groups.title: Routing
groups.question: You are building a product list with filters, pagination and an admin area that only signed-in users can open. Explain how you would set up routing so pages can be shared, refreshed and load quickly.

followUps.Nested routes and URL state: Why should filters and the current page number live in the URL instead of only in component state?
followUps.Lazy routes and guards: How would you stop a signed-out user from seeing the admin page, and keep its code out of the first download?

evidence.text: Routes map URLs to components, and nested routes share a parent layout.
Putting filters and pagination in the URL lets users share links and refresh without losing their place.
URL state also makes the back button return to the previous filter or page.

notEnough: Only saying routes map paths to pages.

evidence.text: Each route's code can be loaded only when the route is visited.
That makes the first load smaller and faster.
A route guard checks if the user is signed in and redirects them before the page renders.

notEnough: Only saying you would protect the route.

misconceptions.text: Says a frontend route guard is enough to keep admin data secure.

groups.title: Forms
groups.question: You are building a checkout form with an email, a card number and an address. Explain how you would validate it so errors are clear and the rules are not duplicated.

followUps.Validation and error states: If the client already validates the form, why must the server validate it again?
followUps.Schema-based validation: How can one schema both validate the form and give you its TypeScript type?

evidence.text: Client-side validation gives quick feedback before submitting.
Server-side validation is still required because anyone can bypass the browser and send requests directly.
Each error message should be linked to its field, for example with aria-describedby, so screen readers announce it.

notEnough: Only saying you validate on both sides.

misconceptions.text: Says client-side validation alone protects the server.

evidence.text: A schema like Zod defines the rules in one place.
The same schema checks the form values at runtime.
The TypeScript type of the form is generated from the schema, so rules and types never drift apart.

notEnough: Only saying you would use Zod.

groups.title: Server State
groups.question: Three components on the same page fetch the same user data, each with its own loading and error code, and the data goes stale after edits. Explain how a server-state library improves this.

followUps.Queries and caching: How does TanStack Query avoid sending the same request three times?
followUps.Stale time and invalidation: After the user edits their profile, how does the profile page get the new data?

evidence.text: Responses are cached by a query key.
Components asking for the same key at the same time share one request.
Stale data is shown immediately and refetched in the background, which replaces hand-written loading and error state.
staleTime decides how long cached data counts as fresh before it is refetched.
After a change, invalidating the related query key tells the cache that data is outdated.
Invalidated queries are refetched so the page shows the new data.

groups.title: Mutations
groups.question: Users click 'like' and wait half a second for the heart to fill in, and some screens show a blank area when the list is empty. Explain how you would make updates feel instant and handle every state of a data view.

followUps.Mutations and optimistic updates: What is an optimistic update and what must happen if the request fails?
followUps.Loading, empty and error states: Why is designing only the success state not enough for a list of orders?

evidence.text: An optimistic update changes the UI immediately, before the server confirms.
If the request fails, the UI is rolled back to the previous value.
The user should be told the action failed instead of silently losing the change.

notEnough: Only saying the UI updates before the server responds.

evidence.text: Every data view has loading, empty, error and success states.
An empty state should explain that there is nothing yet and what to do next.
An error state should say what went wrong and offer a way to retry.

notEnough: Only saying you would add a spinner.
